title: Pinch pot hedgehog figurine
subtitle: A hedgehog in air-dry clay, body from two joined pinch pots
excerpt: A hedgehog figurine about 10 cm long is built from two joined pinch pots forming the body, with a pointed muzzle added as a coil and four small legs pinched from clay blobs. Spines are impressed across the back and sides with a fork before drying. No kiln is needed: the figurine dries at room temperature.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles. Pinch-pot figurine construction is a traditional hand-building approach with no single canonical source. V&A open-access collection for historical ceramic animal figurine form reference.

glossaryTerms.definition: A form made by pressing the thumb into a ball of clay and pinching the walls outward between thumb and forefinger
The joining method: roughen both clay surfaces with a needle, apply clay slip, then press together
The drying stage where clay holds its shape firmly but remains damp enough to join and refine
Fully air-dried and unfired; ready for surface sealing

content.text: A hedgehog figurine about 10 cm nose to tail and 6 cm at its widest sits on a shelf or windowsill as a decorative piece. The body is two
pinch pot

halves joined at the belly, with a shaped muzzle, four small legs, and a pair of tiny ears added before the clay stiffens. Spine texture is pressed into the back and sides with a fork in a close repeating pattern. No kiln is needed: the finished figurine dries at room temperature over two days.

materials.name: Clay slip (same clay body thinned with water)
PVA glue diluted 50/50 with water (for sealing)
Black acrylic paint (for eyes and nose)

content.text: Preparation

Keep a small pot of clay slip ready throughout the session for joining parts. Work quickly: air-dry clay stiffens within 30 to 40 minutes at room temperature. Keep the portion of clay you are not immediately shaping in a sealed bag. Assemble the whole figurine in one session before the body stiffens past the point where parts will bond.
Forming the body halves
Divide the clay into two equal portions of roughly 80 g each. Roll each into a smooth ball. Set aside the remaining clay for the muzzle, legs, and ears.

Form the first pinch pot: press your thumb into the centre of the ball to about halfway through. Pinch between thumb and forefinger, rotating the ball a quarter-turn between each pinch. Work up the walls until you have a dome shape about 6 cm in diameter and 4 cm tall with walls 6-7 mm thick at the base and rim.
Repeat for the second half. The two halves should match in rim diameter. Lay both halves open-side down on a flat board to flatten the base slightly for a stable figurine.
Joining the body and shaping
Use
score-and-slip

on the open rims of both halves. Press the two halves together with the rims aligned to form an oval sphere. Hold for 20 seconds, then gently roll the joined ball in your palms to smooth the equator seam.

Pinch one end of the oval into a blunt pointed muzzle shape by squeezing gently between thumb and forefinger. The muzzle end should be narrow and slightly downturned. The back end of the body stays rounded.
The belly is the flat side where the figurine will sit. Gently press the belly against a flat surface to create a flattened base so the hedgehog stands without rolling.
Adding the features

For the legs: roll four small clay balls roughly 10 mm in diameter. Flatten each into a stubby oval. Score and slip the flat face of each leg and the corresponding position on the belly. Press in firmly, one at each corner of the belly. The legs should stick out enough to lift the body slightly off the surface.

For the ears: roll two tiny clay balls about 6 mm in diameter. Flatten each to a small disc and fold one edge up slightly to create a pinched ear shape. Score and slip to the top of the muzzle end, pressing firmly. The ears sit side by side on the forehead area.
For the nose: press a small clay ball roughly 5 mm in diameter onto the very tip of the muzzle, scored and slipped into place. The nose protrudes slightly.
Impressing the spine texture

While the clay is still soft, press the tines of a fork into the back and upper sides of the body in a repeating close pattern. Each press should leave three or four short parallel lines. Overlap each press with the next to cover the full spine area from behind the ears to the rump, leaving the face, belly, and legs smooth. The fork tines should press in about 1-2 mm for a realistic spine depth.
Drying

Set the hedgehog on a flat board and allow it to air-dry. The figurine is small enough to dry without cracking in most conditions. However, the legs and ears are vulnerable: cover loosely with a cloth for the first 12 hours to prevent the small attachments drying faster than the body and cracking away. The figurine reaches
leather-hard
within four to six hours. At leather-hard you can refine any edges with a wooden rib or add fine detail with a needle tool. Allow to dry fully to
bone-dry
over 24 to 48 hours before painting or sealing.
Finishing

Paint the spine area with a warm brown or dark tan acrylic and the face and belly with cream or pale tan. Paint the nose tip and two small dot eyes in black acrylic. Allow the paint to dry completely. Apply two coats of 50/50 PVA and water across all surfaces to seal and protect.
Use and care

This hedgehog is a decorative shelf figurine. Air-dry clay is not waterproof: keep it indoors away from moisture. Do not wash by immersion. Dust with a dry brush. The legs are the most fragile part: handle by the body rather than the legs.
Variations
Make a small family: a large body at 200 g and two smaller bodies at 80 g each for a mother-and-hoglets grouping on a shared flat slab base.
Use a needle tool to impress individual spine marks at an angle across the back for a more detailed finish, working in rows from the rump forward.
Press a cluster of small clay leaves or a tiny clay mushroom into one front paw at the joining stage to give the hedgehog a foraging prop.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Legs crack away from the body during drying
items.cause: The small attachments dried faster than the main body, causing differential shrinkage at the join
items.fix: Cover loosely with a cloth for the first 12 hours. If a leg breaks off at bone-dry, reattach with PVA glue rather than clay slip

items.problem: Body seam cracks open at the equator
items.cause: The two halves were not at the same moisture level when joined, or the score-and-slip was not thorough
items.fix: At leather-hard, press fresh slip into the crack and smooth. Cover and dry slowly

items.problem: Fork marks look muddy rather than crisp
items.cause: The clay was too wet when the fork was pressed, causing the marks to blur together
items.fix: Wait until the surface just loses its shine before impressing. The clay should hold a sharp indent rather than filling back in after the fork is withdrawn

items.cause: The muzzle end is heavier than the rump due to the nose attachment, or the front legs are shorter than the rear
items.fix: Prop the front legs with a small rolled-clay support while drying. Check leg height when attaching and extend the front legs to match the rear
